title: Remove use of `fmt.Sprintf` of with `slog`
description:
## Description

`fmt.Sprintf()` is used in combination with calls to the `slog` package. This is practice is discouraged when using `slog`. Instead non-static values to include in the log message should be passed to the logger as key value pairs. These uses of `fmt.Sprint()` and `slog` must be removed. [pkg/rscache/file.go#280](https://github.com/rstudio/platform-lib/blob/3462162ff50e6cf0c6d5319d1f868d9b69e21ab2/pkg/rscache/file.go#L278) for an instance of this improper usage.

title: Enable Go StaticCheck linter for platform-lib
description:
## Description

`platform-lib` must enable Go `StaticCheck` linters to detect and warn about common pitfalls / bad practices. The checks performed must match at a minimum the checks enabled for PPM in this [PR](https://github.com/rstudio/package-manager/pull/16273). These checks must be perform via GitHub Actions on every commit and must be capable of running locally on a developer's machine.

title: rslog.CapturingLogger: Messages returns its underlying message slice
description:
The capturing logger returns its underlying message slice, allowing a caller to modify the recorded message contents.

https://github.com/rstudio/platform-lib/blob/8cb8e6209c5f0f7a3aa56ca22568035251baec08/pkg/rslog/capturing_logger.go#L129-L131

https://github.com/rstudio/platform-lib/blob/8cb8e6209c5f0f7a3aa56ca22568035251baec08/pkg/rslog/capturing_logger.go#L143-L148

`Messages()` should return a copy of its message slice.

title: rslogtest.LoggerMock needs synchronization
description: The `rslogtest.LoggerMock` type is not safe to be called from multiple goroutines. In particular, its `stringCalls` field is updated in each call and lacks synchronization.

Fast rsqueue In-progress Work Cancellation
description:
Some deployment strategies require the ability to stop services very quickly. We should support options for rsqueue that enable it to quickly abort in-progress work and return it to the work queue without waiting for a janitor to mark the work as abandoned. 

See the [Twelve-Factor App Disposability Section](https://12factor.net/disposability).

title: Generics for rsqueue and rscache
description: Interacting with the queue and cache can be difficult since we require type registration and casting. Since Go now supports generics, we should research ways to make these interactions simpler and more elegant.

title: Support Azure Blob Storage
description:
Our S3 storage support is useful for a wide variety of providers, but not for Azure Blog storage. We should work on adding support for Azure to the `rsstorage` library.

See https://github.com/rstudio/package-manager/issues/4465. 

A number of cloud providers include S3-compatible APIs:

* [Google Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/migrating)
* BackBlaze B2
* Cloudflare's announced [R2 service](https://blog.cloudflare.com/introducing-r2-object-storage/)
* Smaller cloud provider options: [Digitial Ocean Spaces](https://www.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/), [Scaleway Object Storage](https://www.scaleway.com/en/object-storage/), [Linode Object Storage](https://www.linode.com/products/object-storage/)
* [Minio](https://min.io)

title: Add support for building docker images on ARM architecture
Large Message Chunking for rsnotify
description:
In some situations, notifications sent with `rsnotify` may exceed the 8000-byte Postgres `NOTIFY` limit. We should consider support message chunking in the Postgres (pgx) implementations.

We don't want to encourage abuse of notifications, and notifications, in general, should remain small in size. However, it is ideal to avoid blocking errors in cases where situational parameters cause larger than normal messages. For example, if you add many sources, repos, and subscriptions to Package Manager, it's possible to exceed the 8000-byte limit, although we've rarely encountered this issue.

## Rough Specification

### Sending

When a message is serialized to JSON bytes for sending, if the size exceeds a specific limit, split the message into x-byte chunks and add a prefix:

```
01/03:xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx\n
<first chunk>
```

Since the new header, including the newline, is 43 bytes, we can chunk the message data into 7957-byte chunks. We don't currently provide a message sender implementation, so we'll probably need to add that as well.

### Receiving

When processing incoming messages, if the message beginning matches the chunk header, use the range value (`01/03`) to determine the number of expected chunks, which are cached in memory and reassembled in order before being sent to any subscribers.

## Limits

If a message exceeds a specified number of chunks, err when sending. We can make this limit configurable, or we can use a hard-coded limit like `10`. I recommend keeping the default low since notifications are not ideal for very large messages.

title: Initial Decision Making for Shared Go Components Library
description:
We need to decide how generic the library should be. Should this lib be specific to a specific use case, or should we design it to house future Golang shared code for other uses like shared storage, authentication, etc.? We created a private Google doc for these decisions, which I'll summarize below:


### Should we create single or multiple repos?
We have many ideas for shared Go libraries/components. We need to decide whether to create separate repositories for each library or to house all libraries together in a single codebase. We recommend creating a single repository for shared Go libraries. Given the number of components/libraries that we may eventually create, it will be complicated to maintain separate codebases for each component.
* Separate codebases would require a lot of boilerplate (e.g., end-to-end testing, build, and packaging) for each component.
* Separate codebases would require separate CI pipelines for each component.
* To create example applications for components housed in multiple codebases, we would need to either create a single example that uses multiple modules (complex to manage) or create many example applications (difficult to switch context and manage).
* A good versioning scheme with breaking changes requiring a new major version will support go mod version suffixing (e.g., “/v2”). This will allow consumers to import components of different versions from the same shared codebase if necessary.

### Should we use public or private repo(s)?
We decided on a public repository for several reasons.
* Ease of integration. Avoids difficulty of integrating a private repository for both developers and continuous integration.
* Public contribution. RStudio creates open source software, and this is a way we can contribute to the community. Contributing to open source components that we use in our products will help to ensure that the components/libraries are of high quality.
* No secrets. Platform codebases that are used by multiple products should intentionally avoid including secrets. Any secrets should be kept in product-specific codebases.

### How should we handle versioning?
We should follow the semantic versioning recommendations documented by Go. To summarize:
* Major version changes for a backwards-incompatible change. This would include changes like removing an interface, modifying an interface, or changing an existing behavior in a backwards-incompatible way.
* Minor version changes for a backwards-compatible change, like adding a new function.
* Patch version changes for changes that do not affect a public interface, like bug fixes or optimizations.
* When a version is changed, all lesser versions are reset to zero. Example sequence:
    * 0.6.0
    * 0.6.1
    * 0.8.0
    * 0.8.1
    * 1.0.0
    * 1.1.0
    * 1.1.3
    * 1.2.0
    * 2.0.0
Obviously, using Go’s suggested SemVer scheme conflicts with RStudio’s adoption of CalVer, but I think we should stick with SemVer for go mod compatibility.

### What about packaging?
Shared components will not be packaged. Since this is a shared Go library codebase, we will simply follow best practices for Go modules and any consumers will reference the Github codebase directly.

### Should we support other languages?

We’ve already proven that it’s practical to statically link C++ applications to a Go library, and it’s also possible to use Go libraries from Python. We should keep integration with other languages in mind by developing public interfaces with simple types where practical. However, since our first goal is shared code for Go applications, we should not put a lot of time into supporting other languages from the onset. We will have a few targeted use cases for other languages, and that we can address them on a case-by-case basis.
